notes.b: Aquatics is the Physical Education area built around water. It covers water-based activities that use swimming and/or diving skills and techniques, and every activity in it has a clear reason for being done.
points: Each aquatic activity serves one of three purposes: performance, water safety or recreation. The purpose decides what the activity is trying to achieve.

Performance (competing or presenting to a high standard): racing strokes, water polo (a team ball game played in the water) and synchronised swimming (swimming routines performed to music and judged on composition and skill).

Water safety (staying safe and keeping others safe in and around water): lifesaving (rescuing and caring for people in difficulty in water) and survival swimming (staying afloat and getting to safety yourself).
Recreation: water activity done for enjoyment rather than to compete or to meet a safety need.
notes.tip: Be ready to sort activities by purpose: racing strokes, water polo and synchronised swimming are performance, lifesaving and survival swimming are water safety, and recreation is done for enjoyment.

notes.h: The five options and the choice rule
notes.b: A learner does not have to cover everything in aquatics. The syllabus gives five options and the learner picks one, which becomes the activity they are assessed in.
points: The five options are lifesaving, survival swimming, two swimming strokes, water polo and synchronised swimming. Lifesaving is the specification's own example of an aquatics activity.
Choice rule: a learner selects one of these five options, not several.
The two swimming strokes option means choosing two of the four competitive strokes: front crawl, backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly.
In each activity, learners aim to develop the standard of their performance, be creative and be consistent. Consistent means performing to the same standard each time, not just once.

notes.b: A pool looks safe, but hard wet surfaces and unknown depths cause injuries. Each pool safety rule exists to prevent a particular kind of accident or problem.
points: Swimming takes place under lifeguard supervision, so a trained person is watching and can respond if someone is in difficulty.
Know the depths of the pool before entering the water, so you do not enter or dive where it is too shallow.
No diving in shallow water, because you can hit the bottom and be injured.
Walk, do not run, on the poolside, because wet surfaces are slippery.
Enter the water feet first when the depth is unknown, so your feet find the bottom before your head can hit it.
Follow the pool rules at all times, which are set to keep everyone in the pool safe.
Shower before entering the pool, for hygiene.
notes.tip: Written questions can ask about safety regulations at a pool. Give each rule together with its reason, for example walking because wet surfaces are slippery.

notes.b: The sea, lakes and rivers (open water) are less predictable than a pool and they bring their own dangers, such as cold water and moving water. These rules deal with those extra dangers.
points: Cold water shock: a sudden gasp and rapid breathing when a person enters cold water.
Currents and tides (water flowing in one direction, and the rise and fall of the sea) can carry a swimmer away from the point of entry.
Check the conditions before entering the water, so you know about hazards such as currents and tides before you are in them.
Never swim alone, so that someone can raise the alarm or help if you get into trouble.
Wear a bright swim cap so the swimmer is easy to see from the shore or from a boat.
Swim parallel to the shore rather than straight out from it, so you stay close to safety and do not drift far from where you entered.

notes.b: Aquatics is one of the activities in which a student's practical performance is marked. The assessment looks at more than swimming well: it also tests knowledge of tactics and of safe practice.
points: The performance assessment is worth 30% of the marks and is assessed at common level, meaning the same assessment for Ordinary and Higher Level students.
The State Examinations Commission (SEC, the body that runs the Leaving Certificate) assesses the performance from video.
The chosen aquatics activity is one of the student's three activities.
The assessment covers the listed skills and techniques applied in conditioned (practice set up with set rules or limits), competitive or personal performance.

It also covers tactics (plans used to gain an advantage) or compositional knowledge (how a routine is put together, such as in synchronised swimming), and rules and safe practice before, during and after the activity.

notes.h: Aquatics as a context for theory
notes.b: Written PE questions can use a named activity to test theory, and aquatics provides examples for several topics. Each link below shows how a theory idea appears in swimming.
points: Energy systems (the body's ways of supplying energy to muscles): sprint and distance swimming place different demands on them, because the events differ in length and intensity.
Technique analysis: a stroke is analysed through its body position, arm action, kick, breathing and co-ordination.
Newton's third law of motion: a swimmer pushes water backwards, and the water pushes the swimmer forward with an equal force. This is how propulsion (the forward drive) is produced.
Streamlining: the shape of the body determines how much resistance the water creates, so a streamlined body moves through the water more easily.
Lifeguard as an official: the lifeguard supervises swimmers and enforces the pool's safety rules.
notes.tip: Written questions use aquatics as context: the energy demands of two swimming events, technology helping a swimmer, National Governing Body support (Swim Ireland) and safety regulations at a pool. Answer with the theory applied to swimming, not a general answer.

questions.prompt: Outline three safety rules that apply at a swimming pool and explain why each is needed.
questions.model: Walk, do not run, on the poolside: wet surfaces are slippery, so running greatly increases the risk of a fall and injury. No diving in shallow water: the water may not be deep enough for a dive, so a head or neck injury can result. Enter the water feet first when the depth is unknown: the feet and legs reach the bottom first, so the swimmer can check the depth and avoid striking the head on an unseen bottom.

questions.prompt: Explain how Newton's third law of motion applies to propulsion in swimming.
questions.model: Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. In swimming, the swimmer pushes water backwards with the hands and feet, which is the action. The water pushes back on the swimmer with an equal force in the opposite direction, which is forward, and this is the reaction. This forward force is propulsion, so a stronger backward push on the water produces a larger forward movement.
